rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to observe all 10 compounds, locate their elution window, and identify critical pairs. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in both directions.

Change only gradient duration to measure how the two critical pairs respond to a shallower slope. The current last peak at 7.16 minutes leaves room to improve resolution while likely keeping all peaks within 10 minutes.

The critical pair improved substantially with a shallower gradient. Raising phi0 narrows the gradient window at the same duration, further reducing the slope while trimming early low-organic time to help keep the last peak below 10 minutes.
Lengthen the best gradient by one grid step to push the remaining critical pair toward R ≥ 1.5. The last peak is expected near 9.6 minutes, preserving the zero time penalty.
Injection 4 reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Raise temperature one step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation while measuring the critical pair’s temperature sensitivity.

Test whether higher temperature carries the critical pair through its apparent selectivity crossover and restores separation. The shorter gradient also tests a faster alternative, while injection 4 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Step back from 60 °C to seek a temperature between the two observed selectivity bottlenecks. This may resolve the new close pair while preserving the improved separation of the original critical pair and a last peak below 8 minutes.

Lengthen the 55 °C gradient one step to improve the remaining close pair, while checking that the reordered pair retains adequate resolution. The last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes, potentially matching the maximum score with faster elution than injection 4.

Slightly narrow the gradient window to gain the small resolution increase needed for the R = 1.41 pair. The last peak elutes near 0.54 organic fraction, so this endpoint remains ample and should keep its retention below 10 minutes.

Shift the gradient window upward at its start while keeping nearly the same slope as injection 9, aiming to remove low-organic time without sacrificing critical-pair resolution. Check early-peak retention carefully because the first peak was already at 0.80 minutes.

The higher starting organic fraction damaged selectivity, so test a lower start to strengthen early retention and potentially separate the new critical pair. Combine this with a steeper, shorter gradient to seek full resolution faster than injection 9.

Injection 11 is fully resolved with the last peak at 8.00 minutes. Shorten its gradient by one grid step to test the speed limit while holding the successful starting composition and temperature fixed.

Use a slope between injections 11 and 12 by lowering the endpoint while retaining the 10-minute gradient. This should recover full resolution of the slope-sensitive pair with a last peak slightly earlier than injection 11.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction improves the slope-sensitive pair enough to permit a steeper gradient. This could shorten elution relative to injection 13, while checking that the other critical pair remains resolved.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 14 to lift its R = 1.37 pair above 1.5. The other critical pair has responded weakly to slope, so this may retain full resolution with the last peak earlier than injection 13.

Retain injection 15 as the fastest fully resolved benchmark and explore a faster high-temperature regime. At 60 °C the middle pair has crossed elution order; a steeper gradient may separate it on the opposite side of that crossover.

Test a steeper gradient and higher starting organic fraction to widen the crossed middle pair at 60 °C. Monitor the neighboring pairs for compression; injection 15 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Explore low-temperature selectivity, since the fast 60 °C gradients trade one unresolved pair for another. A broad 10-minute gradient should keep retention manageable while testing whether reordered pairs offer a faster fully resolved alternative.

Test intermediate low-temperature selectivity with a higher starting organic fraction to limit retention time. This explores whether 35 °C separates the central cluster without the severe crowding seen at 25 °C, while retaining the confirmed maximum-score methods as fallbacks.

Trim the unused high-organic portion of injection 15 while preserving its successful gradient slope exactly. Its last peak eluted near 0.57 organic fraction, so a 0.65 endpoint should retain full resolution with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a small slope increase over injection 13, from 0.065 to 0.0667 organic fraction per minute, to refine the boundary of full resolution. This may shorten the separation while preserving the maximum CRF; injection 20 remains the fastest confirmed fallback.

Test the remaining intermediate-temperature regime with a steep gradient, which may separate the original critical pair after its selectivity crossover. The low starting organic fraction protects early retention; injection 20 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Trim injection 11 to an 8-minute gradient while preserving its fully resolving slope and starting composition. Its last peak should remain inside the gradient, offering a compact maximum-score method with slightly more resolution margin than injection 20.

Preserve injection 20’s resolving slope but end the gradient after the first nine peaks, testing a shorter programmed gradient. The isolated last compound will elute during the hold; check whether it still arrives before 10 minutes to preserve the maximum CRF.

Use the final injection to seek a larger resolution margin at the maximum CRF: extrapolating injections 8–9 suggests both critical pairs near R = 1.7 and the last peak below 10 minutes. Injection 20 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
